Thank you for contacting me regarding the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations. I appreciate hearing from you on this important issue.

The Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) is a proposed regional free trade agreement (FTA) being negotiated among the United States, Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, and Vietnam. The United States is negotiating market access for goods, services, and agriculture with countries with which it does not currently have FTAs: Brunei, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, and Vietnam. Comprehensive negotiations are being conducted across 29 separate chapters: intellectual property rights, trade in services, government procurement, investment, rules of origin, competition, labor, environmental standards, and other issues.

The Ministers and Heads of Delegation for their respective countries routinely meet in an effort to negotiate a final treaty. If implemented, the TPP could potentially eliminate tariff barriers to trade and investment among the various parties. A finalized TPP would provide a baseline for future U.S. trade policy in the Asia-Pacific region and beyond. Any FTA that the U.S. reaches a formal agreement on with TPP partners must be approved by Congress through the passage of implementing legislation before taking affect. Additional information pertaining to the TPP can be found here: http://www.ustr.gov/tpp.

I am a strong advocate of free and fair markets, and think that trade agreements have the opportunity to strengthen our economy by creating new global markets and supporting existing ones. Fastest way to ask this question is like this:

I have a space ship. I have breathable air and everything, but the radiator just broke. At what rate per second does every cubic meter of earth-like air lose heat in Celsius, assuming there is no-one and nothing else on board?

I realise I'm asking for an atrociously simplified number here, but can anyone tell me if it can be generalised like this or not?

Edit: I want to add some more data to the question. Thank you to user/NicolaeCeausescu and user/HortManDeux for their responses so far.

  • The starting room temperature is 20 degrees Celcius.
  • We're, let's say, between Sol and Alpha Centauri.
  • Let's say the ship's hull is made of some magical alloy that does not allow heat to escape perceptively.

I'm interested in the interior heat loss when no heat can escape and nothing generates heat.

If it is still unfeasible, is it at least possible to speculate whether I will freeze to death in a matter of minutes, hours, days, months or years (assuming I'm not generating heat)? If heat loss occurs only by radiation, is that generally a fast process or slow one?

Thank you very much in advance!
Ballpark calculation of heat loss of 1m³ oxygen-nitrogen air.
I am not sure I have the capability to answer that question. I would think much would depend on the thermal conductivity of the space ships insulation and if the ship was exposed to sunlight or not.

Your ship will dissipate heat by radiation only. Convection will not occur in a vacuum and presumably your ship is not touching anything so that will negate any conductive losses. In a similar fashion, a running PC would overheat in space it if weren't fitted with some sort of device to radiate the heat.

So, the heat dissipated will depend on the surface area of your ship, what it is made of and what temperature it begins at. It will be described by radiative losses to the surrounding space.

You can't really generalise it much more, without having some hard numbers to work with. As such, this is simply a thought experiment.

There are a lot of factors involved in something like this, as others have said. Even your body is going to produce some amount of heat. Having said that though, I played around with this website a little bit, and it sounds like it's going to be on the order of a few hours before it gets dangerously cold. Depending on the mass of the craft and what it's made of, you could probably increase that to a couple days... maybe?
